There __is__ two pens in the box.
solution:
The correct answer is are.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in "*There **is__** two pens in the box.* " is are.
 
• There ***are ***two pens in the box. 
 
• Here in the given sentence there are two pens, i.e. more than one pen is available in the box.
 
• In the sentence "**is**" should he replaced by "**are**" as *pens is a **plural noun***.
 
• Therefore **option 4 **is the correct option.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Plural noun - **Plural noun is a noun that refers to more than one of something.

 
 
• *For example : "Shells" , "Rooftops" , etc.*
 
 
 
• *​***Plural nouns rules for making sentences:**
 
 
• **​*To make regular nouns plural, add -s to the end.***
 
 
• ​Car= Cars.
 
• House = Houses.
 
 
 
• ***If singular noun ends with -s, -ss, -ch, -x or -z add -es to the end.***
 
 
• ***​***Tax = Taxes.
 
• Church = Churches.
 
 
 
• ***In some cases , singular noun ending in -s or -z, it is required that you double the -s or -z in order to add the -es to make it plural.***
 
 
• ***​***Gas = Gasses.
 
• Fez = Fezzes.
 
 
 
• ***If the noun ends with -f or -fe, the f is somehow changed to -ve before adding -s to them to form plural form.***
 
 
• ***​***Wife = Wives.
 
• Roof = Roofs.
 
 
 
• ***If a singular noun ends with -y we simply add -s.***
 
 
• ***​***Ray = Rays.
 
 
 
• ***If a singular noun ends with -o add -es to make it plural some are exceptions to them just add -s.***
 
 
• ***​***Potato = Potatoes.
 
• Photo = Photos.
 
 
 
• ***If a singular noun ends with -us add -i at end.***
 
 
• ***​***Cactus = cacti.
 
 
 
• ***If a singular noun ends with -is add -es.***
 
 
• ​Analysis = Analyses.
 
 
 
• ***If a singular noun ends with -on add -a.***
 
 
• ***​***Phenomenon = Phenomena.
 
 
 
• ***Some nouns don't change when they are pluralized.***
 
 
• ***​***Sheep = Sheep.
 
• Series = Series.

__
 
• "**By giving so many**" is grammatically **correct**.
 
• The **preposition** **"by"** is used to show **how work is done**.
 
 
• **Example:*** Mike travels **by** bus. *
 
 
 
• The **verb "giving**" is in the correct form of a tense, which is **present continuous** because the action is going on. 
 
 
• **Example:** *Sera is **giving** massages at a nearby parlour.* 
 
 
 
• The **phrase "so many"** denotes the **unspecific quantity**. 
 
 
• **Example:** *Martha has **so many** works left undone. *
 
 
 
• As the phrase "by giving so many" justifies its usage, no substitution is required. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• A **sentence** must justify the **subject-verb concord** to be grammatically correct. 
 
• **The subject** is the **noun or pronoun** about which the sentence is. 
 
• Subject-verb concord means the **subject and verb must agree in number.**
 
• If the **subject is singular**, the **verb** should also be **singular** and if the **subject** is **plural**, the **verb** must also be **plural**. 
 
 
• **Example:** *The **boys want** to play cricket but **she wants** to play basketball. *

subject: ENG
question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

__Unless we sat__ in an incorrect posture, we may strain our back.
solution:
The correct answer is: If we sit.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• 'If' is used in sentences in which one thing only happens or is true when another thing happens or is true.
 
• In this context, it is said that if someone sits in an incorrect posture (one thing happens), he/she may strain his/her back (another thing happens).
 
• Also, the sentence is a **conditional sentence. **A conditional sentence begins with 'If'.
 
• If the condition is in the **present tense **(sit), then its result should be in the **future** (denoted by 'may').
 
• The incident that happens first or was supposed to happen first takes a **present tense** (sit) when ‘will/shall/can/may’ is present in the main clause (strain).

Therefore, the correct answer is: ***If we sit***__ in an incorrect posture, we may strain our back.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• The three types of conditional sentences (with examples) are given in the table.

 
 

 I
 If I study
 I may pass the exam
 
 

 II
 If I studied
 I might pass the exam
 
 

 III
 If I had studied
 I might have passed the exam

Father asked me __that if I will__ accompany him to the park.
solution:
The correct answer is** 'whether I would****'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

**The phrase "asked me that if I will" is incorrect because it incorrectly uses direct speech formatting in an indirect speech sentence.**

**Here are the rules:**

 
• **Indirect questions:** When we turn direct questions into indirect ones, we have to consider the tense used in direct speech. If it's present, the tense generally changes to the past in the reported speech. In your sentence, 'will' should become 'would'.
 
• **Usage of 'if' and 'whether'**: We usually use 'if' or 'whether' to report yes/no questions. However, 'whether' is more formal and is often used in writing or in more formal speaking. Moreover, **'whether' can be used before infinitives, but 'if' cannot.** When you're expressing doubt between alternatives, '**whether' is the correct choice.**
 
• **The conjunction 'that':** In reported speech, 'that' is often used as a conjunction to join the reporting verb to the rest of the sentence. But when the sentence is a question, we don't use 'that', we generally use 'if' or 'whether'. Therefore, in your sentence, the conjunction 'that' is wrongly used.

The correct sentence should be: "Father asked me** whether I would** accompany him to the park."

**Here, "whether" is used because it's a yes/no question and the verb tense has been changed from 'will' to 'would' because the direct question is being reported indirectly.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When two subjects are linked by words like '**along with**', '**together with**', '**as well as**', etc., the verb agrees with the first subject. Therefore, we use **is** or **was,** or **has** instead of **are**, **were,** or **have**.

 
 
• *Example- The director **along with** his wife **has** come to our house.*
 
• Example- He **as well as** his daughter **sings** well. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• This is known as subject-verb-agreement of a sentence where the **subjects and verbs agree with each other in terms of number** (singular or plural).
 
• If the subject of a sentence is **singular** the verb of that sentence should also be **singular**.
 
• If the subject of a sentence is plural the verb of that sentence should also be plural.
 
• There are many subject-verb-agreement rules in English Grammar.

• **The correct sentence: **"The District Collector, Mr Kaushalendra Kumar, is visiting the site for inspection" would be the correct sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **"Option 2".**

question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

What __is the qualities__ of a good teacher?
solution:
The correct answer is: "**are the qualities**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The sentence "What is the qualities of a good teacher?" contains an error. 
 
• The error is in subject-verb agreement. The word "**qualities**" is a plural noun, and the verb that follows should also be in the plural form, which is "**are**."
 
• In the original sentence, the singular verb "**is**" is used, which does not agree in number with the plural noun "qualities."
 
• **Subject-verb agreement** is a grammatical rule that dictates that the verb in a sentence must agree in number with its subject.
 
• In this case, when the subject is plural, as in "qualities," the verb should also be in the plural form, such as "are."
 
• **Corrected Sentence**: *What are the qualities of a good teacher?*
 
• In this corrected sentence, "**are**" matches the plural noun "**qualities**," resulting in correct subject-verb agreement.

Therefore, **option 3** is the correct answer.

question:
Select the correct option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution'.

It is __more hot now.__
solution:
The correct answer is** option (3)** i.e. **"hotter now".** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **"more hot now__**" is grammatically incorrect. It should be **"hotter now."**
 
• **‘hot’** is an adjective. It has three degrees. **Hot** (positive), **Hotter **(comparative) and **Hottest **(superlative).
 
• The adjectives that have comparative forms **do not need to add ‘more’ before them.**
 __
 
• **For example: Better (CORRECT), More good (INCORRECT), Quicker (CORRECT), More quick (INCORRECT).**
 
 
 
• Hence, the correct answer is "hotter now".

Therefore the correct sentence is " It is hotter now__". [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• The adjectives that do not have any comparative forms** need to add ‘more’ before them.** Generally, adjectives with two or more than two syllables take more before them.

 
 
• **For example: Beautiful- More beautiful**. **Boring- More boring. **

 [IMAGE: //cdn.testbook.com/resources/lms_creative_elementsadditional-information-image.png] **Additional Information__**

• Adjective-noun arrangements in English require careful choice to ensure the adjectives accurately describe the nouns.

options.text: was able to find out a solution

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**__Key Points__**

• The sentence uses the correlative conjunction **Neither... nor** to join two subjects: **the chairman** and **the members**.
 
• According to the rule of **subject-verb agreement**, when subjects are joined by **either... or** or **neither... nor**, the verb must agree with the **closest subject** (the second subject).
 
• In this sentence, the second subject is **the members of the committee**, which is **plural**.
 
• Therefore, the singular verb **was** must be replaced with the plural verb **were** to ensure grammatical correctness.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'Neither the chairman nor the members of the committee **were able to find a solution** to the pressing issue.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Proximity Rule:** This rule states that the verb should agree with the noun or pronoun closest to it when using connectors like **or**, **nor**, **either... or**, and **neither... nor**.
 
• **Option 1:** **was able to find out a solution** – Incorrect because it retains the singular verb **was**.
 
• **Option 3:** **had been able to find for a solution** – Incorrect because the phrase **find for** is idiomatically wrong in this context; the verb **find** does not require the preposition **for** when looking for a result.

question:

It's none uncommon to find street musicians playing in the park during the weekends, drawing crowds from nearby areas.

options.text: nothing uncommon to find street musicians
not uncommon to find street musicians
never uncommon to find streets of musicians

solution:
The correct answer is __**not uncommon to find street musicians**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The phrase **'none uncommon'** used in the original sentence is grammatically incorrect because **'none'** is a pronoun or an adverb meaning **'not any'** or **'to no extent'**, and it cannot properly modify the adjective **'uncommon'** in this specific sentence structure.

• The correct expression **'not uncommon'** is a rhetorical device known as **litotes**, where a negative statement (not) is used to affirm a positive sentiment (common); it suggests that the event occurs with reasonable **frequency**.

• In the structure **'It is'** (contracted as **'It's'**), the word **'is'** acts as a **linking verb** which must be followed by an adjective or an **adjectival phrase**; the adverb **'not'** is the standard tool for negating such adjectives in English.

• The term **'street musicians'** is a correctly formed **compound noun** referring to individuals who perform music in public spaces for tips, fitting the context of the sentence perfectly.

 **Additional Information__**

• **'Nothing uncommon'** vs. **'Not uncommon'**:

• **'Nothing'** is a **pronoun**. While one could say **'There is nothing uncommon about this'**, it does not fit the **dummy subject** structure of **'It is...'** as effectively as the adverb **'not'**.

• **'Never uncommon'** and **'Streets of musicians'**:

• **'Never'** is an **adverb of frequency** meaning **'at no time'**; using it here would create an absolute statement that is stylistically unusual for describing a casual weekend observation.

• The phrase **'streets of musicians'** uses a **prepositional phrase** that changes the meaning entirely, suggesting the physical roads are populated by or belong to musicians, rather than describing the **buskers** themselves.

solution:
The correct answer is __**keeps reverting to her bad habits**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence contains a grammatical error known as **redundancy** or **pleonasm**. This occurs when a word is used that repeats the meaning already contained within another word in the same phrase.

• The verb **revert** is defined as returning to a former state, practice, habit, or condition. The prefix **re-** in Latin-based words typically signifies **back** or **again**.

• Because the concept of moving **back** is already inherent in the definition of **revert**, adding the word **back** immediately after it is unnecessary and considered incorrect in **formal English**.

• Option 1 provides the correct improvement by removing the redundant adverb **back** and maintaining the prepositional phrase **to her bad habits**, making the sentence concise and grammatically sound.

• Options 2 and 3 are incorrect because **reverting backward** remains redundant, and **reverting forth** is logically contradictory, as **forth** implies forward movement which opposes the meaning of **revert**.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Common Redundancies**:

• **Return back**: To return means to come or go back; therefore, **back** is extra.

• **Reply back**: To reply is to answer back, making **back** redundant.

• **Added bonus**: A bonus is something added, making the word **added** unnecessary.

• **End result**: A result occurs at the end, making **end** redundant.

• **Etymology of Revert**:

• Originates from the Latin word **revertere**, where **re-** means back and **vertere** means to turn.

• In legal contexts, it refers to **reversion**, where property returns to the original owner or their heirs after a specific period or event.

• In **software engineering**, to **revert** a commit means to undo changes and return the code to a **previous state**.

• The use of **would** in the **if-clause** is grammatically incorrect. Instead, the **subjunctive mood** should be used to express a hypothetical condition.
 
• The phrase **were to be** is a formal way to express a hypothetical future event in the subjunctive mood, perfectly matching the main clause **I would seriously consider**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **were to be laid off again**.

• Parallelism is essential when using coordinating conjunctions like **and** to link phrases. Using a mixture of **gerunds** and **infinitives** in one series results in **faulty parallelism**.

• **Verbs Followed by Gerunds**:

**__Key Points__**

__

• The adjective **conducive** means making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible. In English grammar, it is a **fixed collocation** that this word is always followed by the preposition **to**. Therefore, phrases like 'conducive in' or 'conducive of' are idiomatic errors.

• When the word **to** acts as a preposition (as it does following the adjective 'conducive'), any subsequent verb must be in the **gerund form** (verb + ing). This explains why **bringing** is required instead of the base form 'bring'.

• The phrase **bring stability to** is the standard idiomatic construction used to indicate the recipient or the system affected by the stabilization. The preposition **to** correctly identifies the **financial system** as the entity receiving the benefit of the measures.

• The original sentence is incorrect because it uses the preposition 'in' after 'conducive', fails to use the **gerund** form of the verb, and uses the wrong preposition before 'the financial system'.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Prepositional Idioms:**

• Certain adjectives require specific prepositions to be grammatically correct. Examples include **detrimental to**, **beneficial to**, and **immune to**.

• **Conducive to** is frequently used in formal reports and academic writing to describe factors that contribute to a desired environment or result, such as **economic growth** or **peace**.

• **Gerund vs. Infinitive:**

• Learners often mistake the **prepositional to** for the **infinitive marker to**. In phrases like 'look forward to', 'object to', or 'conducive to', the word **to** is a preposition and must be followed by a **noun** or **gerund**.

• Example: 'The environment is **conducive to** learning' (Noun) or 'The environment is **conducive to** studying' (Gerund).

• The underlined part **'can't help feel'** is a variation of an **idiomatic expression** that typically requires either a **gerund** or a specific **conjunction** to be considered grammatically standard in formal written English.

• The expression **'cannot help'** is an idiom meaning to be unable to refrain from or avoid a particular action, **emotion**, or **impulse**.

• When using this idiom with a **bare infinitive** (the base form of a verb like 'feel'), the conjunction **'but'** must be placed between 'help' and the verb. This creates the standard construction **'cannot help but [verb]'**.

• In this structure, **'but'** functions as a **restrictive preposition** meaning 'except'. Therefore, the phrase **'can't help but feel'** literally implies that the speaker is unable to do anything except feel sorry for the individual.

• While the original phrasing **'can't help feel'** is occasionally used in **informal speech**, it is technically incomplete. Option 1 provides the necessary grammatical bridge required for standard English usage.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Linguistic Structures of the Idiom:**

• **Gerund Construction:** One of the most common standard forms is **'cannot help + [verb]-ing'**. For example, 'I **cannot help feeling** sympathy.' This is widely used in both **British English** and **American English**.

• **Double Negative Function:** The construction **'cannot help but'** is technically a **double negative** that functions as an **affirmative**. It is often preferred in literary and **formal contexts** to emphasize a lack of choice.

• **Grammatical Avoidance:**

• **Solecisms:** It is important to avoid mixing these two rules. Phrases such as **'cannot help but feeling'** (mixing 'but' with a gerund) or **'cannot help from'** are considered **grammatical errors**.

solution:

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase **once-in-a-lifetime** is a standard **idiomatic expression** and a **compound adjective** used to describe an event that is exceptionally rare, unique, or likely to happen only once.
 
• In the original sentence, the phrase **once-in-the-lifetime** is used. This is grammatically incorrect because the standard idiom requires the **indefinite article** (a) within the hyphenated structure to denote any single lifetime, rather than the **definite article** (the).
 
• Linguistically, the word **once** begins with the vowel letter **o**, but it is phonetically pronounced starting with the **consonant sound** **w** (/wʌns/).
 
• According to **English grammar rules**, the article **a** is used before words that begin with a **consonant sound**, while **an** is reserved for words beginning with a **vowel sound**. Therefore, **a once-in-a-lifetime** is the only phonetically and idiomatically correct choice.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Phonetic Article Selection**:
 
 
• The choice between **a** and **an** depends on the **initial sound** of the next word.
 
• Words starting with vowel letters but **consonant sounds** include **a university** (/juː/) and **a one-way street** (/wʌn/).
 
• Words starting with consonant letters but **vowel sounds** include **an hour** (/aʊər/) and **an honor** (/ɒn.ər/).
 
 
 
• **Hyphenation Rules for Compound Adjectives**:
 
 
• A **compound adjective** (like **once-in-a-lifetime**) is a group of words that functions as a single unit to modify a noun (**opportunity**).
 
• These are **hyphenated** when they precede the noun they modify to prevent **ambiguity** and help the reader identify the group as a single descriptive unit.
 
• If the adjective follows the noun (e.g., The opportunity was once in a lifetime), the hyphens are usually omitted.

__The reason why I am confused is because__ they are giving me mixed signals.

options.text: Why am I confused is because
The reason for my confusion is because

solution:
The correct answer is __**I am confused because**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence contains a **redundant** expression, also known as a **pleonasm**. The phrase **the reason** and the **subordinating conjunction** **because** both indicate **causality**. Using them together in a single clause is considered **tautological** in standard English.
 
• The word **reason** acts as a noun that points to a cause, while **because** introduces the cause itself. Grammatically, 'the reason' should be followed by a **complement clause** starting with **that** (e.g., 'The reason is that...'), not an adverbial clause starting with 'because'.
 
• Option 3, **I am confused because**, provides the most **direct** and **concise** way to convey the message. It eliminates the **wordiness** of the original sentence by removing the unnecessary subject phrase 'The reason why'.
 
• In **Sentence Improvement** tasks, the goal is to choose the option that is both **grammatically accurate** and **stylistically superior**. Simplifying the structure to **Subject + Verb + Conjunction** ensures clarity and follows the **principle of economy** in language.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Analysis of incorrect options:
 
 
• **Why am I confused is because**: This option incorrectly uses an **interrogative word order** ('Why am I') within a **declarative sentence**. Furthermore, it retains the **redundancy** between 'Why' and 'because'.
 
• **The reason for my confusion is because**: While it replaces 'why I am confused' with a **noun phrase**, it fails to correct the fundamental **grammatical error** of pairing 'reason' with 'because'. A correct alternative would have been 'The reason for my confusion is **that**'.
 
• **Redundancy Rule**: Common redundant phrases often tested include 'return back', 'reason why... because', 'repeat again', and 'sufficient enough'. Removing the repetitive element is a standard **error detection** strategy.
 
• **Conjunction usage**: **Because** is a **subordinating conjunction** that connects a dependent clause to an independent clause. When the purpose of the sentence is to state a fact directly, starting with the subject is preferred over complex **nominalizations**.
 
 
</ul

• The sentence follows a **past tense** narrative structure, established by the main reporting verb **concluded** and the subsequent linking verb **was**.

• To maintain **tense consistency** and **parallelism** within the subordinate clause, the second action (governed by the same subject **policy**) must also be in the **simple past tense**. Therefore, **required** is the correct form to match **was**.

• Option 1 correctly combines the idiomatic preposition **with** and the past tense verb **required**, ensuring the sentence is both grammatically sound and logically consistent.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Understanding Prepositional Collocations:**

• **Replete with:** Formal term used for abundance or being full (e.g., a book **replete with** illustrations).

• **Full of:** A more common alternative, but specifically requires the preposition **of**.

• **Fraught with:** Typically used when something is filled with negative elements like **danger**, **difficulties**, or **risks**.

• **Abounding in/with:** Used to indicate that something exists in large numbers or amounts.

• **Tense Sequencing Rules:**

• When the **Principal Clause** is in the **Past Tense**, the **Subordinate Clause** must also be in the **Past Tense**, unless it expresses a universal truth or a habitual action.

• In this sentence, the need for **revision** is a specific past consequence of the **panel's** finding, necessitating the use of **required** over **requires** or **requiring**.

options.text: decided for hiring a cruise ship
decided to hire a cruise ship

solution:
The correct answer is __**decided to hire a cruise ship**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence contains a **syntactic error** in the phrase 'to for hire'. In English grammar, an **infinitive marker** 'to' should be followed directly by the **base form** of the verb. The inclusion of the preposition 'for' between the infinitive marker and the verb creates a **redundancy** and violates standard **word order** rules.
 
• The verb **decide** is a **transitive verb** that typically requires a **to-infinitive** (to + verb) when it is used to express a choice or a resolution to perform a specific action. The structure **decided to hire** correctly follows this linguistic pattern, where 'to hire' serves as the **infinitive phrase** acting as the object of the decision.
 
• In this context, the term **hire** functions as a verb meaning to obtain the use of something for a fee. By removing the unnecessary preposition 'for', the sentence achieves **grammatical clarity** and logical flow, making 'decided to hire a cruise ship' the only syntactically sound replacement.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Infinitive vs. Gerund Collocations**:
 
 
• Specific verbs in English are followed by either an **infinitive** or a **gerund** (verb + -ing). Verbs like **decide**, **plan**, **agree**, and **hope** are strictly followed by infinitives.
 
• Option 1 ('decided for hiring') is incorrect because it uses a **prepositional gerund phrase** where a **to-infinitive** is required. The verb **decide** does not collocate with the preposition 'for' when followed by an action.
 
 
 
• **Prepositional Usage of For**:
 
 
• The preposition **for** is generally used to indicate **reason**, **purpose**, or **duration**. While one can 'decide for' a specific noun (e.g., 'decided for the blue car'), it is not used to introduce a verbal action in the same way an **infinitive** does.
 
• Option 3 ('decided for a cruise ship') removes the verb **hire** entirely, which changes the intended meaning of the sentence from the act of renting a vessel to simply choosing the vessel itself.
 
 
</ul

options.text: The rigorous training program, having been completed by the employees

Having completed the rigorous training program, the employees

solution:
The correct answer is __**Having completed the rigorous training program, the employees**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence contains a grammatical error in the formation of the **perfect participle**. The structure **having completing** is incorrect because the auxiliary verb **having** must be followed by the **past participle** (V3) form of the verb, which is **completed**.

• The **perfect participle** (having + past participle) is specifically used to denote an action that was finished before another action began. Here, the completion of the **rigorous training program** occurred prior to the employees feeling **well prepared**.

• The correct choice places the **participle phrase** at the beginning of the sentence. This creates a clear **introductory modifier** that logically refers to the subject **the employees**, who appear immediately after the comma.

• By restructuring the sentence this way, the **syntactic flow** is improved, removing the awkward parenthetical interruption found in the original sentence and ensuring the **chronological sequence** of events is clearly communicated.

• This correction adheres to the rules of **subject-modifier agreement**, where the person or thing performing the action in the participle phrase must be the grammatical subject of the main clause.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Participle Phrases**:

• **Perfect Participle**: Formed by **having + past participle**. It indicates a completed action (e.g., **Having finished** the work, he left).

• **Present Participle**: Formed by **V-ing**. It usually indicates an action happening simultaneously with the main verb (e.g., **Walking** down the street, I saw him).

• **Misplaced and Dangling Modifiers**:

• A **misplaced modifier** occurs when the descriptive phrase is too far from the noun it modifies. In Option 1, the **rigorous training program** is the subject, which would imply the program itself **felt well prepared**, resulting in a logical error.

• A **dangling modifier** happens when the intended subject of the modifier is missing from the sentence entirely.

• **Passive Voice Construction**:

• Option 1 uses a **passive perfect participle** (having been completed), which unnecessarily complicates the sentence and shifts the focus away from the **employees** as the active participants.

</ul

Using **fully** with **tired** is considered a weak **collocation** and is less common in formal or idiomatic writing.

• The phrase **hardly any energy left** serves as a critical **contextual clue** in the sentence. This **quantifier** indicates a near-total absence of **stamina** or physical resources, which aligns exactly with the definition of **exhaustion**. Therefore, **exhausted** provides a more **economical and precise** description of the students state than the original underlined phrase.

• From a **syntactic perspective**, replacing a multi-word phrase with a single, potent **synonym** improves the **conciseness** and **flow** of the sentence. This is a common principle tested in **sentence improvement** tasks to evaluate a candidates **vocabulary depth** and **stylistic awareness**.

• The original sentence structure establishes a **cause-and-effect** relationship where the **long hike** and the **steep hill** (the stressors) resulted in a specific physical state. **Exhausted** effectively bridges these components by emphasizing the **severity** of the fatigue resulting from **arduous physical activity**.

The intensifier **too much** is typically used before **uncountable nouns** (e.g., too much noise) or to modify **verbs** (e.g., he talks too much). You need to come to terms with the fact that you have lost your chance and there's no going back.

options.text: come at terms of the fact
come on terms with the facts
come in terms to the fact

solution:
The correct answer is __**No improvement required**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The underlined phrase **'come to terms with'** is a fixed **idiomatic expression** in English which means to gradually **accept** a sad or difficult situation or to find a way to live with it.
 
• This idiom follows a strict **syntactic structure** consisting of the verb **'come'**, the prepositional phrase **'to terms'**, and the preposition **'with'**. Any deviation from these specific prepositions results in an **ungrammatical** or **non-idiomatic** construction.
 
• In the sentence provided, the object of acceptance is **'the fact'**, referring to the specific situation of losing a chance. The use of the **definite article** 'the' before the singular noun 'fact' is logically and grammatically sound because it identifies the **propositional content** that follows (that you have lost your chance).
 
• Because the original sentence correctly utilizes the **standard idiom** and maintains **proper prepositional usage**, it does not require any stylistic or grammatical changes. The integrity of the **clause structure** and the **semantic meaning** are both intact.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Analysis of incorrect prepositional combinations:
 
 
• **'Come at terms of'**: This is incorrect because **'at terms'** is not a recognized phrase for acceptance; **'at'** usually denotes a specific location or point in time, and **'of'** fails to show the relational bond required by the idiom.
 
• **'Come on terms with'**: Although the phrase **'on good terms'** exists to describe a friendly relationship, it cannot substitute **'to terms'** when describing the psychological process of **resignation** or acceptance.
 
• **'Come in terms to'**: This is often confused with **'in terms of'** (meaning regarding), but **'in terms'** cannot be paired with the verb **'come'** to convey acceptance. Furthermore, **'terms'** must be followed by **'with'** to correctly link to the situation being accepted.
 
 
 
• The word **'terms'** in this context relates to **'conditions'** or **'provisions'**, suggesting that the person has reached a state where they can coexist with the **harsh conditions** of their reality.

was able to attended the conference
were able to attend the conference

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence uses the correlative conjunction **neither...nor** to join two subjects: **the manager** and **his assistants**.
 
• According to the **Rule of Proximity**, when subjects are joined by **neither...nor** or **either...or**, the verb must agree with the subject closest to it.
 
• In this sentence, the closer subject is **his assistants**, which is **plural**. Therefore, the verb must also be plural.
 
• The singular verb **was** must be replaced with the plural verb **were** to ensure **subject-verb agreement**.
 
• Additionally, the past tense must be maintained to match the context provided by the phrase **which was disappointing**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'Neither the manager nor his assistants **were able to attend the conference**, which was disappointing for the entire team.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** 'is able to attend' is incorrect because it uses a **singular verb** and changes the tense to **present**, which contradicts the past tense used in the rest of the sentence.
 
• **Option 2:** 'was able to attended' is incorrect because **was** is singular, and the phrase **to attended** violates the rule of infinitives (**to + base form of the verb**).
 
• **Option 4:** 'No improvement required' is incorrect because the original sentence contains a **subject-verb agreement error** where a singular verb is paired with a plural subject.
</ul

• The original sentence contains a grammatical error in the verb form used within a **passive voice** construction.
 
• In English grammar, the **passive voice** for the simple past tense follows the structure: **Subject + was/were + past participle (V3) + by + agent**.
 
• The word **implement** is the base form of the verb. Its **past participle** form is **implemented**.
 
• Since the **new policy** is the receiver of the action performed by the **government**, the verb must be in its past participle form after the auxiliary verb **was**.
 
• Thus, the correct phrase is **was implemented by the government**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'The new policy **was implemented by the government** after extensive consultations with experts from various fields.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: 'was implementing by the government'** – This uses the **present participle** (-ing form), which denotes an active continuous action. It does not fit the passive structure required here.
 
• **Option 3: 'implemented by the government'** – This removes the helping verb **was**, which is necessary to form the **passive voice** in this specific sentence structure.
 
• **Option 4: 'No improvement required'** – This is incorrect because the base form **implement** cannot follow the auxiliary **was** in this context.
</ul

options.text: would have taken stronger action earlier

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence provided is a perfect example of a **Third Conditional** sentence, which is used to describe a hypothetical situation in the **past** that did not happen.
 
• The standard grammatical structure for a Third Conditional is: **If + Past Perfect (had + past participle), ... would have + Past Participle**.
 
• In the conditional clause (the 'if' clause), the phrase **'had taken'** is the **Past Perfect** form of the verb 'take', which correctly sets up the past hypothetical condition.
 
• The result clause correctly uses **'would have been'** (would have + past participle of 'be'), indicating the hypothetical outcome in the past.
 
• Because the underlined portion **'had taken stronger action earlier'** follows the required grammatical rules for this structure, no changes are necessary.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'If the government **had taken stronger action earlier**, the economy would have been in a much better position to recover from the crisis.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** 'took stronger action earlier' – This uses the **Simple Past** tense. This would only be used in a **Second Conditional** (hypothetical present/future), which would require the main clause to be 'the economy would be...' instead of 'would have been'.
 
• **Option 2:** 'would have taken stronger action earlier' – In English grammar, **'would have'** is almost never used in the **'if' clause**; it is reserved for the result clause.
 
• **Option 3:** 'was taking stronger action earlier' – This is the **Past Continuous** tense, which describes an ongoing action in the past rather than the completed hypothetical condition required for the Third Conditional.
</ul

• **Historical Origins**:

• The word **verbose** is an adjective used to describe a person or piece of writing that uses **more words than are needed**. It is the most appropriate term to describe a book that is being criticized for its length or repetitive nature.
 
• The original sentence contains a **prepositional error** by using **to being** instead of the correct gerund phrase **for being**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Understanding the distinctions between similar-sounding words is crucial for **sentence improvement**:
 
 
• **Verbose**: This refers to **wordiness** or **prolixity**. It carries a negative connotation in literary criticism when a book is unnecessarily long.
 
• **Verbal**: This pertains to **words** in general or **spoken** rather than written communication. Saying a book is **excessively verbal** is semantically redundant as all books consist of words.
 
• **Vocal**: This describes someone who expresses their **opinions freely and loudly**. While a person can be vocal, a book itself cannot be described as **excessively vocal** in the context of being wordy.

The prestigious award was given to the scientist for his groundbreaking research in genetics.
solution:
The correct answer is __**groundbreaking research in genetics**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **groundbreaking** is a **compound adjective** that characterizes **scientific research** or **pioneering discoveries** that represent a significant **innovation**; it metaphorically refers to **breaking new ground** in a specific **academic discipline**.
 
• **Genetics** is the **biological science** that studies **heredity**, **genes**, and **genetic variation** in organisms; the term was formally coined by the **British biologist William Bateson** in **1905**.
 
• In **formal English**, **research** is typically treated as an **uncountable noun**, and the **prepositional phrase** **in genetics** correctly identifies the **scientific field** or **domain** of the **scientist's** work.
 
• The **original sentence** is **grammatically sound** as the word **groundbreaking** is the most **idiomatic** and **formal** choice for describing **award-winning research**, making this phrase the **correct choice** for the sentence.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Groundshaking and Genetic**
 
 
• **Groundshaking**: This **adjective** usually describes **literal seismic activity** (earthquakes) or **metaphorical shocks** that cause **great surprise**, but it is not the standard **collocation** used for **academic research**.
 
• **Genetic**: This is an **adjectival form** (e.g., **genetic engineering**); when referring to the **entire field of study**, the **noun** **genetics** (with the **-ics** suffix) must be used.
 
 
 
• **Common Errors**
 
 
• **Orthographic Errors**: Terms like **groundbraking** are **misspellings**; **braking** refers to **slowing down a vehicle**, while **breaking** refers to **shattering** or **opening** something.
 
 
</ul

A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option which can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."
The reforms were introduced with the hope that they would catalyse an atmosphere conducive of innovation and inclusivity.
solution:
The correct answer is __**conducive to innovation or inclusivity**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The primary error in the original sentence lies in the **prepositional collocation**. In standard English, the adjective **conducive** is strictly followed by the preposition **to** when indicating that a situation or environment makes a particular outcome likely.

• The phrase **conducive of** is considered non-standard or archaic in modern usage; therefore, the replacement must utilize the **to-infinitive** structure or a prepositional phrase starting with **to**.

• The sentence requires **parallelism**, a grammatical principle where items in a series must share the same grammatical form. In the correct option, **innovation** and **inclusivity** are both **abstract nouns**, maintaining the logical balance of the sentence.

• While the original sentence used the conjunction **and**, the option **conducive to innovation or inclusivity** is the only one that corrects the fundamental idiomatic error while preserving the **noun-noun** parallel structure.

• In the context of **economic and social reforms**, creating an atmosphere that is **conducive to** progress is a common **idiomatic expression** used to describe facilitating growth or development.

 **Additional Information__**

• Analysis of Incorrect Options:

• **conducive of innovations with inclusiveness**: This option fails because it retains the incorrect preposition **of** and changes the meaning by using **with**, which does not effectively link the two goals to the atmosphere being created.

• **conducive to innovate and inclusivity**: This choice violates the **rule of parallelism**. It attempts to pair the **verb** **innovate** with the **noun** **inclusivity**. For a sentence to be grammatically sound, both elements linked by **and** or **or** should be of the same **part of speech** (i.e., both nouns).

• **No improvement required**: This is incorrect because the original phrase **conducive of** is a **grammatical error** that must be corrected to **conducive to**.

• Key Definitions:

• **Innovation**: The practical implementation of ideas that result in the introduction of new goods or services or improvement in offering goods or services.

• **Inclusivity**: The policy or practice of providing equal access to opportunities and resources for people who might otherwise be excluded or marginalized.

</ul

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

• The primary error in the sentence is the incorrect use of an **apostrophe** in the possessive pronoun '**theirs**'.
 
• **Possessive pronouns** such as **theirs**, **ours**, **yours**, **hers**, and **its** never take an apostrophe.
 
• The word '**theirs**' functions as a **possessive pronoun** here, standing in for the phrase '**their production plan**' to avoid repetition.
 
• The use of the **comparative degree** '**more sustainable**' is appropriate because the sentence compares two distinct production plans.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'I am confident that our production plan is **more sustainable than theirs**.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** '**their**' is a **possessive adjective** and requires a noun immediately following it (e.g., 'more sustainable than **their plan**').
 
• **Option 3:** '**most**' is the **superlative** form, used when comparing three or more things; here, only two are being compared. Additionally, '**theirs'**' is not a valid word in English.
 
• **Possessive Pronouns vs. Adjectives:** Possessive pronouns (**mine**, **ours**, **yours**, **his**, **hers**, **its**, **theirs**) replace a noun phrase, while possessive adjectives (**my**, **our**, **your**, **his**, **her**, **its**, **their**) modify a noun that follows them.

• Option 3 is incorrect because while **aim for** can be used with a noun, **aimed at** is the preferred and more formal construction when describing the objective of systemic **reforms** or policies followed by a verb.

 **Additional Information__**

• Understanding Phrasal Verbs with **Bring**:

• **Bring about**: To make something happen, especially a **major change** or **revolution**.

• **Bring up**: To mention a subject or to **rear children**. Example: She was **brought up** in a small town.

• **Bring forward**: To introduce for **discussion** or to change the **timing** of a meeting to an earlier slot.

• **Bring in**: To introduce a **new law**, system, or **legislation**.

The chairman reaffirmed again his commitment to enhancing the organisation's financial transparency and accountability.
solution:
The correct answer is __**reaffirmed his commitment**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The verb **reaffirm** is defined as stating or asserting something strongly **once again**. The prefix **re-** in English grammar inherently denotes **repetition** or a return to a previous state.
 
• Using the word **again** in conjunction with **reaffirmed** creates a **pleonasm**, which is the use of more words than are necessary to convey a meaning. This is considered a **redundancy error** in formal writing.
 
• In the original sentence, the phrase **reaffirmed again** essentially translates to **affirmed again again**, which is grammatically incorrect. Removing the word **again** streamlines the sentence and adheres to the rules of **grammatical economy**.
 
• The structure **reaffirmed his commitment** is the most **precise** and **concise** choice, maintaining the **Subject-Verb-Object** flow while effectively conveying that the **chairman** is stating his dedication a second time.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Redundant Phrases in English:**
 
 
• **Option 1 (reaffirmed his commitment again):** Moving the word **again** to the end of the phrase does not eliminate the **semantic overlap**. It remains redundant because the **re-** prefix already carries the meaning of **again**.
 
• **Option 2 (reiterated once again):** The verb **reiterate** means to say something **repeatedly** for emphasis. Combining it with **once again** creates an even more wordy and **redundant** expression than the original sentence.
 
• Common examples of similar errors include **return back**, **revert back**, **recede back**, and **repeat again**. In all these cases, the adverb (back/again) should be omitted for **grammatical correctness**.
 
 
 
• **Contextual Usage:** In **professional communication** and **corporate governance**, using **exact terminology** like **reaffirmed** is preferred to show **consistency** and **transparency** in leadership actions.
</ul

A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
He studied all night for the exam but failed to remember nothing the next day.
solution:
The correct answer is __**failed to remember anything**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence contains a **double negative** error. In English grammar, using two negative words in the same clause typically results in a positive meaning, which contradicts the intended context of the sentence.
 
• The verb **failed** already carries a negative implication (the inability to achieve an action). Pairing it with the negative pronoun **nothing** creates a logical fallacy suggesting the subject remembered something.
 
• To express a total lack of recall, the negative verb must be followed by the **non-assertive** indefinite pronoun **anything**. This structure maintains the negative sense required by the conjunction **but**, which indicates a contrast between studying all night and the poor outcome.
 
• Grammatically, **failed to remember anything** is equivalent to the phrase **remembered nothing**. However, since **failed** is already part of the sentence structure, **anything** is the only appropriate choice to complete the thought logically.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Usage of Indefinite Pronouns:**
 
 
• **Anything:** This is an **indefinite pronoun** used primarily in **negative sentences**, questions, and conditional clauses. It serves as the counterpart to **something** in non-affirmative contexts.
 
• **Nothing:** This is used in affirmative sentences to give them a negative meaning (e.g., 'I have nothing'). Combining it with words like **failed**, **without**, or **scarcely** is a common stylistic error.
 
 
 
• **Contextual Logic of Other Options:**
 
 
• **Failed to forget everything:** This would logically imply that the person managed to remember everything, which is semantically opposite to the failure suggested by the context of a difficult exam situation.
 
• **Failed to forget anything:** This suggests a **perfect memory** or total recall, which does not align with the narrative of struggling after a long night of study.
 
 
</ul

A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."
The new policy was believing to have reduced corruption in the department.
solution:
The correct answer is __**was believed to have reduced**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The subject of the sentence is **The new policy**, which is an inanimate object. An inanimate object cannot perform the cognitive action of **believing**. Therefore, the **active voice** (was believing) is logically incorrect, and the sentence requires a **passive voice** construction (was believed).

• The phrase **to have reduced** is a **perfect infinitive**. This grammatical structure is used to indicate an action that occurred prior to the time of the main verb. In this sentence, it signifies that the **reduction of corruption** is a completed action relative to the time people held the belief.

• The **past passive** form **was believed** correctly establishes the timeframe of the public or departmental opinion, while the **perfect infinitive** properly links it to the preceding outcome of the policy.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Passive Voice Mechanics**:

• In English grammar, the **passive voice** is formed using the auxiliary verb **to be** followed by the **past participle** (V3) of the main verb. Here, **was** (be-verb) + **believed** (V3) correctly shifts the focus to the policy as the object of belief.

• **Stative Verbs and Continuous Tense**:

• The verb **believe** is a **stative verb** (expressing a state of mind). Stative verbs are generally not used in **continuous tenses** (e.g., was believing, is being believed) in formal standard English, making such options grammatically weak.

• **Simple vs. Perfect Infinitive**:

• A **simple infinitive** (to reduce) usually refers to the same time as the main verb or a future time. A **perfect infinitive** (to have reduced) refers to a time earlier than the main verb. Given the context of a policy already showing results, the **perfect infinitive** is the most precise choice.

</ul

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

• The sentence describes a sequence of events in the **past**. When two actions happen in the past, the action that was completed first is expressed in the **Past Perfect Tense** (had + past participle).
 
• The phrase **by the time** is a strong indicator that the **Past Perfect** should be used to show that the decisions were finished before the director's arrival.
 
• Since the **decisions** are the recipients of the action, the **Passive Voice** of the Past Perfect is required: **had been + past participle (made)**.
 
• Therefore, the underlined part **were made** should be replaced with **had been made** to correctly reflect the timeline of events.

Therefore, the correct answer is **1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'The meeting had already started, and **several key decisions had been made** by the time the new director arrived.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: "several keys decision were made"** – This is grammatically incorrect because **keys** is used as an adjective here and should be singular (**key**), and **decision** should be plural (**decisions**) to match the quantifier **several**.
 
• **Option 3: "several keen decisions was made"** – This contains a **subject-verb agreement** error; the plural subject **decisions** requires the plural verb **were** or **had been**, not the singular **was**. Additionally, **keen** changes the intended meaning of the sentence.
 
• **Option 4: "No improvement required"** – This is incorrect because the **Simple Past** (were made) does not clearly establish the completion of the action before the director's arrival as accurately as the **Past Perfect** does in a formal grammatical context.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Understanding Idiomatic Precision**:

• **Fixed Phrases**: English contains many **paired idioms** where prepositions are not repeated, such as **by leaps and bounds** or **part and parcel**. Altering these established structures usually results in **non-standard English**.

• **Redundancy**: In formal writing, **brevity** is prioritized. Repeating 'in' does not add new meaning and is therefore removed to achieve a **sharper sentence structure**.

• **Analysis of Incorrect Forms**:

A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
They decided to discard their original plans, which was formed without taking its potential long-term consequences into account.

options.text: which was formed without taking their potential
which were formed without taking their potential
which were formed without taking its potential

solution:
The correct answer is __**which were formed without taking their potential**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **relative pronoun** 'which' refers directly to the **antecedent** **plans**. In English **syntax**, the verb following a relative pronoun must agree in number with its antecedent. Because **plans** is a **plural noun**, the singular auxiliary verb **was** is grammatically incorrect and must be replaced by the plural form **were**.

• The **possessive pronoun** within the clause also refers back to the **plural noun** **plans**. The singular possessive pronoun **its** is only used for singular non-human entities. To maintain **pronoun-antecedent agreement**, the plural possessive **their** must be used to correctly attribute the **long-term consequences** to the multiple plans.

• The original sentence contains a **number disagreement** error where a plural subject is paired with a singular verb and a singular pronoun. The improved phrase **which were formed without taking their potential** rectifies both grammatical inconsistencies.

• By using the plural forms, the sentence logically conveys that each of the **original plans** had potential consequences that were initially overlooked.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Subject-Verb Agreement**:

• This rule dictates that the **verb** must match the **subject** in person and number. For plural nouns like **plans**, **strategies**, or **ideas**, plural verbs such as **were**, **are**, or **have** are required.

• **Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement**:

• An **antecedent** is the noun or pronoun to which a subsequent pronoun refers. 

• **Its**: Used for a singular **neuter** antecedent (e.g., the company, the car).

• **Their**: Used for any **plural** antecedent (e.g., the companies, the cars, the plans).

• **Relative Clauses**:

• A **defining** or **non-defining relative clause** (starting with 'which' or 'that') functions as an adjective. The **grammatical integrity** of the sentence depends on the clause mirroring the properties of the noun it modifies.

</ul

A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
Three-fourth of the cake has been eaten by the guests, and the remaining portion will be served to the kitchen staff later.

options.text: Three-fourth of the cake have been eaten
Three-fourths of the cake has been eaten
Three-fourths of the cake have been eaten

solution:
The correct answer is __**Three-fourths of the cake has been eaten**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Pluralization of Fractions**: In English grammar, when a fraction has a **numerator** greater than 1 (such as 2, 3, or 5), the **denominator** must be in its plural form. Therefore, while we say **one-fourth**, we must say **three-fourths**.

• **Subject-Verb Agreement with Fractions**: When a fraction is followed by the preposition **of**, the **verb** agrees with the noun that follows the preposition. If the noun is **singular** or **uncountable**, a **singular verb** is used. If the noun is **plural**, a **plural verb** is used.

• **Analysis of the Noun**: In this sentence, the noun following the fraction is **cake**, which is **singular**. Therefore, the auxiliary verb must also be **singular**. The singular auxiliary verb **has** is the correct choice to accompany **cake**.

• **Grammatical Consolidation**: The original sentence used **Three-fourth**, which lacks the necessary plural suffix **-s** for the denominator. The correct improvement must include both the pluralized denominator and the singular verb **has**.

• Therefore, the option **Three-fourths of the cake has been eaten** is the correct one.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Countable vs. Uncountable Contexts**:

• If the sentence referred to multiple separate cakes, such as **three-fourths of the cakes**, the verb would change to **have** to maintain agreement with the plural noun.

• The word **cake** in this context refers to a single whole item being partitioned, thus necessitating **has**.

• **Hyphenation Rules**:

• While the provided answer does not use a hyphen, it is common in formal writing to hyphenate fractions when they function as **adjectives** (e.g., a **three-fourths** share). When acting as a **noun**, the hyphen is often omitted, though usage varies between style guides.

• **Fractional Proportions**:

• This rule applies to all proportions, including **percentages**. For example, **fifty percent of the cake has** been eaten, but **fifty percent of the guests have** arrived.

</ul

When scaling the Himalayas, the higher one ascends, the lesser oxygen is available.
solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence follows the structure of **parallel comparison** (also known as a correlative or proportional comparison).
 
• This structure requires the pattern: **The + comparative adjective/adverb + subject + verb, the + comparative adjective/adverb + subject + verb.**
 
• In the first part, **higher** is the comparative degree of **high**. Therefore, the second part must also use a comparative degree.
 
• The comparative degree of **little** (used for uncountable nouns like oxygen) is **less**.
 
• While **lesser** is also a comparative, it is typically used as an attributive adjective to mean **of smaller size, value, or importance** (e.g., the lesser of two evils). When referring to the **amount or quantity** of something like oxygen, **less** is the grammatically correct choice.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'When scaling the Himalayas, **the higher** one ascends, **the less** oxygen is available.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: the least oxygen is available** – This is incorrect because **least** is a superlative degree, whereas the correlative structure requires a comparative degree.
 
• **Option 3: the oxygen available is lesser** – This is incorrect because it breaks the parallel **The + comparative** structure required at the beginning of the clause.
 
• **Option 4: No improvement required** – This is incorrect because **lesser** is not standard in this specific correlative context comparing quantity; **less** is the appropriate term.
</ul

The original phrase **added fuel in the fire** uses the incorrect preposition **in**.

• The word **ambitious** (showing a strong desire for success) does not logically contrast with the intention to **pacify** (to calm or soothe). In a **diplomatic context**, remarks that are **ambiguous** (vague or open to multiple interpretations) are a common cause of escalating **tensions** because they lead to **misunderstanding** and **mistrust**.

• Option 3 is incorrect because **assiduous** means showing great care and **perseverance**; such remarks would unlikely result in the worsening of a situation.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Ambiguous**:

• Originates from the Latin **ambiguus**, meaning **doubtful**.

• Key characteristic: It describes a **statement** or **sign** that can be understood in more than one way, often leading to **confusion** in **negotiations** or **legal documents**.

• **Antagonistic**:

• Derived from **antagonismos** (Greek), meaning **struggle**.

• Key characteristic: Shows active **opposition** or **hostility** toward someone or something.

• **Assiduous**:

• Refers to a person or action showing **meticulous** attention and **constant** effort.

• Key characteristic: Highly valued in **academic** and **professional** settings for **thoroughness**.

• **Pacify**:

• To bring **peace** to a state of **turmoil** or **war**.

• Core function: It is a **transitive verb** often used in **international relations** and **conflict resolution**.

The novel's plot was so intricate and captivating, it was impossible for the reader to predict the ending.
solution:
The correct answer is __**that it was impossible**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The sentence requires the use of a **correlative conjunction** to link the degree of an attribute to its result. The standard structure used in English for this purpose is **so + adjective/adverb + that**.

• In this context, **so** modifies the adjectives **intricate** and **captivating**, while the word **that** introduces the **subordinate clause** explaining the consequence (the impossibility of predicting the ending).

• While the word **that** is occasionally omitted in informal spoken English, formal writing and competitive examinations require its inclusion to avoid a **comma splice** and to clearly establish the **cause-and-effect** relationship.

• By replacing the comma and the following phrase with **that it was impossible**, the sentence achieves grammatical completeness and logical flow.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Correlative Structures**:

• **So... that**: Used with adjectives or adverbs to show degree and result (e.g., **so fast that**).

• **Such... that**: Used with **noun phrases** to show degree and result (e.g., **such an intricate plot that**).

• **Too... to**: Used to indicate a negative consequence due to excess (e.g., **too intricate to predict**).

• **Analysis of Incorrect Options**:

• **so it was impossible**: This creates a **redundancy** because the word **so** is already present earlier in the sentence. Using it twice as a conjunction and an intensifier in this manner is non-standard.

• **as to not be possible**: This phrase follows the **so + adjective + as to + verb** construction. However, it is wordy, less direct, and typically used when the subject of both clauses is the same. In the original sentence, the **reader** (implicit or explicit) is the one facing the impossibility, making the **that clause** more appropriate.

</ul

The poor villagers are unable to cope up with the rising cost of living.

options.text: not able to cope up with

solution:
The correct answer is __**unable to cope with**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The phrase **cope with** is a standard **English phrasal verb** that means to deal effectively with something difficult, to manage a stressful situation, or to endure a hardship.

• The usage of **cope up with** is a common **grammatical error** often found in Indian English, likely resulting from a confusion between the two distinct idioms **cope with** and **keep up with**.

• In formal **linguistic structures**, the preposition **up** is considered redundant and incorrect when paired with **cope**; the verb **cope** is intransitive and traditionally only takes the preposition **with** to connect to its object.

• The sentence requires the removal of the unnecessary word **up** to ensure **syntactic precision**, making **unable to cope with** the only grammatically sound replacement for the underlined segment.

• The context of the sentence involves the struggle of **poor villagers** against the **rising cost of living**, which refers to an **inflationary pressure** or economic challenge that one must manage or endure.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Cope with** vs. **Keep up with**:

• **Cope with**: Focuses on the **psychological** or **physical capacity** to handle a burden or a difficult task (e.g., coping with grief or financial loss).

• **Keep up with**: Focuses on **maintaining the same pace**, level, or progress as another entity (e.g., keeping up with the neighbors or keeping up with the news).

• **Redundancy in Phrasal Verbs**:

• Many errors in competitive examinations involve **superfluous prepositions**. Just as **cope** does not require **up**, verbs like **await** do not require **for**, and **comprise** does not require **of** in the active voice.

• The word **cope** originates from the **Old French** word **couper** (to strike or cut), evolving in English to signify a successful 'contending' or 'struggle' against something.

</ul

• Option 2 is incorrect because **Despite** is never followed by the preposition **of**. While **In spite of** is a three-word preposition, **Despite** functions as a single-word preposition on its own. Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.

While reduced clauses exist, **Despite** is the most direct and standard choice for preceding a gerund phrase in this context. Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Despite**: Used without **of**. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or **gerund**.
 
• **In spite of**: Meaning is identical to despite, but it must include **of**.

• **Although / Even though / Though**: These are followed by a **clause** (Subject + Verb). Example: **Even though** they faced challenges, they finished.

Unless traffic rules are not made more stringent, such terrible accidents will continue to occur.

options.text: If traffic rules are not made more stringent
Until traffic rules are not made more stringent
Till traffic rules are not made more stringent

solution:
The correct answer is __**If traffic rules are not made more stringent**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence contains a **double negative** error. The word **Unless** is a **subordinating conjunction** that means **if... not** or **except if**.
 
• Since **Unless** already carries a negative meaning, it should not be followed by another negative word like **not** in the same clause. Doing so creates a logical contradiction that fails to convey the intended condition.
 
• To correct this, we can either remove the word **not** (e.g., **Unless traffic rules are made...**) or replace **Unless** with **If** while keeping the negative **not**.
 
• The option **If traffic rules are not made more stringent** correctly establishes the **conditional clause**. It indicates that the failure to make rules stricter will result in the continuation of accidents.
 
• The structure **If + subject + negative verb** is a standard way to express a negative condition in English grammar, making it the most suitable replacement for the underlined part.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Understanding Conjunctions:**
 
 
• **Unless**: Used to express a **negative condition**. It is followed by an **affirmative verb**. Example: **Unless you work hard, you will not succeed**.
 
• **If... not**: This is the functional equivalent of **unless**. Example: **If you do not work hard, you will not succeed**.
 
• **Until/Till**: These are **temporal conjunctions** used to refer to a **point in time** or the duration of an action. They mean **up to the time that**. Using them in this context is incorrect because the sentence requires a **condition**, not a **time limit**.
 
• **Stringent**: This adjective means **strict**, **precise**, and **exacting**. In the context of **traffic rules**, it refers to the implementation of firm regulations to ensure safety.
 
 
</ul

• When the word **need** is used as a noun to indicate that something is required or necessary, it is most commonly followed by the preposition **for**.
 
• The standard **collocation** is **need for** something (e.g., the need for change, the need for speed).
 
• The expression **need of** is generally reserved for the idiom **in need of**, which describes a state of lacking something essential.
 
• Thus, the phrase **need for stronger regulations** is the grammatically correct improvement for the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'The chairman emphasized the **need for stronger regulations** to curb financial fraud.'*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: 'need in stronger regulations'** – This uses an incorrect preposition. **Need** does not take **in** when expressing a requirement for an object.
 
• **Option 3: 'need to stronger regulations'** – The preposition **to** is used after **need** when followed by a **verb** (infinitive form, e.g., 'need to implement'), but not when followed directly by a **noun phrase** like 'stronger regulations'.
 
• **Option 4: 'No improvement required'** – This is incorrect because **need of** is less appropriate than **need for** in this context of expressing a formal requirement.
</ul

subject: ENG
question:
Choose the sentence that is in simple past tense:

A. I was giving some of the chocolates to my younger sister.

B. I had been giving some of the chocolates to my younger sister.

C. I had given some of the chocolates to my younger sister.

D. I gave some of the chocolates to my younger sister.
solution:
The correct answer is 'Option 2: I gave some of the chocolates to my younger sister.'

 

Key points:

 

Simple past tense is used to talk about a completed action at a certain time in the past. It only requires the past form of the verb.

The sentence "I gave some of the chocolates to my younger sister" uses the verb 'gave' which is the simple past form of 'give' indicating a completed action.

The other options involve past continuous, past perfect continuous, and past perfect tenses which do not fit the requirement for simple past tense.

Additionally, Simple past tense does not use auxiliary verbs which we see present in the options a), b), c. Therefore, the correct answer is 'Option 2: I gave some of the chocolates to my younger sister.'

Additional Information:

 

Option A ("I was giving some of the chocolates to my younger sister") is in the past continuous tense. It denotes an ongoing action in the past.

Option B ("I had been giving some of the chocolates to my younger sister") is in the past perfect continuous tense. It refers to an action that started in the past and continued up until another time in the past.

Option C ("I had given some of the chocolates to my younger sister") is in the past perfect tense. It is used for an action completed before another point in the past.

The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Pure chance led my friend Hercule Poirot, formerly chief of the Belgian force, to be connected with the Styles Case. 

A. Having been wounded on the Somme and invalidated out of the Army, I finally took up my quarters with him in London. 

B. In doing so, I feel that I cannot do better than begin with that strange tangle which aroused such widespread public interest at the time. 

C. Since I have a firsthand knowledge of most of his cases, it has been suggested to me that I select some of the most interesting and place them on record. 

D. His success brought him notoriety, and he decided to devote himself to the solving of problems in crime. 

S2. I refer to the affair at the Victory Ball.
solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph begins by describing the origin of **Hercule Poirot**'s career as a private detective following a specific case. 
• **Sentence D is the first sentence** as it provides a direct consequence of the **Styles Case** mentioned in S1: 
• 'His success brought him notoriety, and he decided to devote himself to the solving of problems in crime.' 
• **Sentence A follows** as it introduces the narrator's personal background and explains how he came to reside with Poirot in **London**: 
• 'Having been wounded on the Somme and invalidated out of the Army, I finally took up my quarters with him in London.' 
• **Sentence C is the third sentence** because it builds on the narrator's proximity to Poirot, explaining that his **firsthand knowledge** led to the suggestion that he record the cases: 
• 'Since I have a firsthand knowledge of most of his cases, it has been suggested to me that I select some of the most interesting and place them on record.' 
• **Sentence B is the fourth** as the phrase 'In doing so' refers back to the act of recording cases mentioned in C, and it introduces a specific **strange tangle**: 
• 'In doing so, I feel that I cannot do better than begin with that strange tangle which aroused such widespread public interest at the time.' 
• The final fixed sentence S2 completes the thought by identifying the case as the affair at the **Victory Ball**. 
• The correct sequence is **DACB**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'Pure chance led my friend **Hercule Poirot**, formerly chief of the Belgian force, to be connected with the **Styles Case**. His success brought him **notoriety**, and he decided to devote himself to the solving of problems in crime. Having been wounded on the **Somme** and invalidated out of the **Army**, I finally took up my quarters with him in **London**. Since I have a **firsthand knowledge** of most of his cases, it has been suggested to me that I select some of the most interesting and place them on record. In doing so, I feel that I cannot do better than begin with that **strange tangle** which aroused such widespread public interest at the time. I refer to the affair at the **Victory Ball**.'</div

S1. The country in which Richard found himself
solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph describes the arduous and secretive journey of **Richard** through a foreign land back to his home in **England**.
 
• **Sentence D follows S1** because it provides immediate detail about how Richard navigated the **wild and rough country** mentioned in the first sentence:
 
 
• 'Alone and quietly he made his way through **woods and over mountains**, not daring to tell who he was.'
 
 
 
• **Sentence A follows D** as it provides the justification for his secrecy and fear of being recognized:
 
 
• 'For in those **rude times** no stranger was safe in a foreign land and a **shipwrecked king** would have been a fine prize.'
 
 
 
• **Sentence C follows A** because the word **'So'** indicates the consequence of the danger mentioned in A, describing his disguise:
 
 
• 'So, as a **poor pilgrim** returning from the **Holy Land**, he trudged onward, looking very **ragged and forlorn** and keeping out of the way of people as much as he could.'
 
 
 
• **Sentence B follows C** as it elaborates on the daily struggles of his journey as a pilgrim before concluding with the final fixed sentence S2:
 
 
• 'Now and then he found **food and lodging** at the hut of some **poor woodsman**, but often he had **no shelter** under which to rest at night.'
 
 
 
• The correct sequence is **DACB**.
